q: In Nevada, who is responsible for supervising a salesperson's real estate activities?
options: The broker the salesperson is associated with
wrong: The Commission regulates but doesn't supervise day to day.
why: The associated broker supervises salespersons and broker-salespersons.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: A Nevada salesperson may receive compensation for real estate work from:
options: The buyer directly, if the buyer agrees
wrong: Payment must flow through the broker.
Party consent doesn't change the rule.
Title companies don't pay agents directly.
why: All compensation goes through the broker.

q: A Nevada salesperson may accept a bonus directly from a seller as long as the broker is told afterward.
wrong: Any compensation must come through the broker, not directly from a party.
why: False.

q: A salesperson's association with a broker is made official by:
options: Filing it with the Real Estate Division
Notifying the local REALTOR® association only
wrong: A verbal deal isn't recognized by the Division.
Social media doesn't establish licensing status.
Association membership is separate from licensing.
why: Association is recorded with the Division.

q: A Nevada broker can be disciplined for failing to supervise a salesperson who broke the law.
wrong: Failure to supervise is itself a ground for discipline.
why: True. Brokers answer for supervision.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: A Nevada salesperson can be associated with how many brokers at one time?
wrong: A salesperson works under one broker.
why: A salesperson works under a single broker.

q: A licensee buys a home for themselves from a private seller. What must they do?
options: Disclose in writing that they hold a real estate license
Nothing, since it's a personal purchase
Use an unlicensed friend to negotiate
wrong: License status must be disclosed even on personal deals.
That avoids nothing and adds unlicensed activity.
why: Licensees disclose their license status when dealing for themselves.

q: A neighbor sends you a buyer who closes on a home. You want to thank the neighbor with part of your commission. What should the agent do?
options: Don't share commission with an unlicensed person; ask your broker what's allowed
Pay them a cash referral fee
Pay them after the license renewal
wrong: Paying unlicensed people for licensed work is prohibited.
Routing it through the buyer is still improper.
why: Commissions can't be shared with unlicensed people for licensed activity.

q: You're new and unsure how to fill in a counteroffer. What should the agent do?
options: Ask your broker or a designated supervisor before sending it
Ask the other agent to fill it in for you
Copy an old contract from another state
wrong: The other agent represents the other side.
Other states' forms may not fit Nevada.
why: Supervision exists for exactly this.
hook: When in doubt, ask your broker.

q: You're leaving your brokerage for another. Your listings were signed with the old broker. What should the agent do?
options: Understand the listings belong to the broker; work out any transfer with both brokers and the clients
Take the listings with you automatically
Tell clients to cancel and re-sign without telling the broker
Keep marketing them under the new brokerage
wrong: Listing agreements are with the broker, not the agent.
Inducing cancellations behind the broker's back is improper.
You can't advertise another broker's listings.
why: Brokerage agreements belong to the broker.

q: A listing agreement is between the client and the broker, not the individual salesperson.
wrong: Brokerage agreements are with the broker.
why: True.

q: A Nevada salesperson wants to open a brokerage in their own name. What is required?
wrong: A PM permit is for management, not running a brokerage.
CE keeps a license current; it doesn't upgrade it.
Salespeople must work under a broker.
why: Only brokers can operate a brokerage.

q: A broker-salesperson must work under the supervision of a broker.
wrong: A broker-salesperson holds broker qualifications but works under another broker.
why: True.

q: The brokerage receives a $12,000 commission. The salesperson's split is 70%, paid by the broker. How much does the salesperson receive?
formula: Agent share = brokerage commission × agent split
why: The broker pays the salesperson's share: $8,400.

q: Which Nevada statute governs how brokers deposit and account for money held for others?
why: NRS 645.310 sets deposit and accounting rules.
hook: Deposit it right, record it all.

q: Earnest money a Nevada licensee receives is usually deposited:
options: In the broker's trust account or with the escrow holder named in the agreement
wrong: The seller doesn't hold deposits before closing.
why: Trust or escrow, as the agreement and law provide.
hook: Trust or escrow, never your pocket.

q: Commingling client money with a broker's own funds is a ground for discipline in Nevada.
wrong: Commingling is listed as a ground for discipline.
why: True.
hook: Lie, mix, hide, or pay the unlicensed: discipline.

q: Using a client's deposit to pay brokerage rent is called:
wrong: Mixing funds is commingling; spending them is conversion.
Escrow is neutral holding of funds.
why: Spending trust money for your own use is conversion.
hook: Mixing is commingling. Spending is conversion.

q: The Real Estate Division may inspect and audit a broker's trust account records.
why: True.
hook: If it isn't recorded, it didn't happen.

q: Commonly cited Nevada rules require brokers to keep transaction records for at least how long? [verify]
why: Commonly cited as 5 years. Check the current rule.

q: A buyer hands you an earnest money check on Saturday. What should the agent do?
options: Give it to the broker or deliver it to escrow as the agreement and NRS 645.310 require, and document it
Hold it in your car until the deal closes
Deposit it in your own account
wrong: Holding funds indefinitely violates deposit rules.
The deposit must be handled promptly, not held.
why: Get it into trust or escrow promptly and keep a record.
hook: Deposit it right, record it all.

q: A deal falls apart and both buyer and seller demand the earnest money held in trust. What should the agent do?
options: Tell the broker; the funds stay put until the parties agree in writing or a court or the contract's process decides
Give it to whichever party asks first
Keep it as a fee for the trouble
why: Disputed funds stay in trust until properly released.

q: Why might a Nevada broker keep a small amount of their own money in a trust account?
options: Only if allowed, to cover bank service charges
wrong: Trust accounts aren't for broker investment.
Agent pay comes from operating funds.
why: Rules may allow a limited amount to cover bank fees. [verify]

q: Failing to keep required trust records can be a violation even if no money is missing.
wrong: Record keeping is a separate requirement.
why: True.
hook: If it isn't recorded, it didn't happen.

q: A trust account holds deposits of $5,000, $3,500, and $10,000. A $3,500 deposit was released at closing. What should the trust balance be?
why: The ledger should show $15,000.
hook: Deposit it right, record it all.

q: A tenant pays you a security deposit in cash for a property your broker manages. What should the agent do?
options: Give a receipt, turn it over to the broker, and make sure it's recorded and deposited to trust
Hold it in your desk until the lease ends
Use it for repairs right away
wrong: The broker handles funds per the management agreement.
why: Receipt, broker, trust, record.
hook: Trust or escrow, never your pocket.

q: Put the earnest money steps in order.
options: The agent receives the buyer's check
The agent gives it to the broker or escrow holder
It's deposited to trust or escrow
The deposit is recorded in the ledger
why: Receive, deliver, deposit, record.
hook: Deposit it right, record it all.

q: A Nevada salesperson may keep client funds in their own account until the broker asks for them.
wrong: Salespersons must turn funds over promptly for proper deposit.
why: False.
hook: Trust or escrow, never your pocket.

q: Nevada real estate advertising must include:
why: Ads must identify the licensed brokerage.

q: A licensee's social media post about a listing counts as advertising.
why: True. Any medium, same rules.

q: An ad for a listing that shows only "Call 702-555-0100" with no brokerage name is a:
options: Blind ad, which Nevada doesn't allow
Legal ad if the number is the agent's
wrong: Licensee ads must identify the brokerage.
The number doesn't replace the brokerage name.
A net listing is a pricing arrangement.
why: Blind ads hide that a licensee is advertising.

q: A Nevada team's ads can use only the team name, without the brokerage name.
wrong: Team ads must still show the brokerage.
why: False.

q: Can a licensee advertise another broker's listing on their own website?
options: Only with the listing broker's permission
Yes, any MLS listing is fair game
Yes, if they take out the brokerage name
wrong: Removing the brokerage makes it worse.
why: You need the listing broker's permission.

q: Which ad claim is most likely to be misleading?
options: "Guaranteed to double in value in 2 years"
why: Guaranteeing future value is a false promise.

q: You're selling your own condo by owner. What should your ad include?
options: A statement that you hold a Nevada real estate license
Nothing extra, since it's your own home
A note that no agents may call
wrong: Hiding identity isn't the issue; disclosure is.
why: Licensees advertising their own property disclose their license.

q: You're setting up an Instagram account to market your real estate business. What should the agent do?
options: Include your brokerage's licensed name and keep posts accurate
Use a nickname only so it feels personal
Post other brokers' listings to grow followers
Leave the brokerage off since it's social media
why: Same advertising rules apply online.

q: A broker is responsible for supervising the advertising of licensees associated with the brokerage.
why: True.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: You helped a buyer purchase a home but didn't list it. You want to post "Just sold!" What should the agent do?
options: Make your role clear, such as "Represented the buyer," and follow your broker's policy
Use the listing agent's photos without asking
Post the seller's sale price and reasons for selling
why: Accurate claims about your role, with permissions respected.

q: A licensee's name in an ad should appear:
options: As it's licensed with the Division
As any nickname they like with no licensed name
It may be left out entirely if the brokerage is shown
wrong: Ads shouldn't create confusion about who is licensed.
When an agent is named, it should match the license.
why: Use the name on file with the Division. [verify details]
hook: Advertise the name on your license.

q: False or misleading advertising can lead to discipline in Nevada.
wrong: Misrepresentation in ads is a ground for discipline.
why: True.

q: A yard sign for a Henderson listing shows the agent's name and phone. What else must it show?
why: Every ad, including signs, shows the brokerage.

q: You plan to text past clients about a new listing. What should the agent do?
options: Identify your brokerage, keep it accurate, and follow consent rules for texting
Send it from an anonymous number
Exaggerate the features to get responses
Skip the brokerage name to save characters
wrong: Brevity doesn't excuse leaving it out.
why: Texts are advertising too.

q: Which is a ground for discipline under Nevada law?
options: Referring a client to a lender with disclosure
wrong: Disclosed referrals aren't misconduct by themselves.
why: Misrepresentation is a listed ground.
hook: Lie, mix, hide, or pay the unlicensed: discipline.

q: Making a false promise to influence a client is a ground for discipline.
why: True.

q: Acting for more than one party in a transaction without written consent is:
options: Allowed if both parties are friends
Allowed if the commission is reduced
why: Multiple representation needs written consent (Consent to Act).
hook: Two clients? Get it in writing.

q: Failing to cooperate with a Division investigation can be disciplined on its own.
why: True.

q: Which can lead to discipline even outside a real estate transaction?
options: Buying a home with a mortgage
wrong: That's allowed when done through the Division.
why: Certain convictions are grounds for discipline.
hook: Conduct counts outside the deal too.

q: In Nevada, failing to comply with a court order for child support can affect a license because:
options: State law allows license action for unpaid support orders
It's a federal real estate rule
why: Nevada law ties professional licenses to support compliance. [verify]
hook: Conduct counts outside the deal too.

q: A seller asks you not to mention a known roof leak to buyers. What should the agent do?
options: Explain you must disclose known material defects and can't hide it
Agree, since the seller is your client
Mention it only if asked twice
Cover it with fresh paint before showings
wrong: Duties to the client don't allow concealing known defects.
why: Known material defects must be disclosed.
hook: Disclose it before they find it.

q: A home inspector offers you $200 for each client you send. What should the agent do?
options: Decline undisclosed compensation; any arrangement needs disclosure and your broker's approval and must be legal
Accept and tell the client after closing
wrong: Undisclosed referral pay is a conflict of interest.
Disclosure after the fact doesn't fix it.
why: No secret profits; disclose and follow your broker.

q: Telling a buyer "this home will definitely be worth 30% more next year" is acceptable sales talk.
wrong: A definite promise about future value is a false promise.
why: False.

q: A broker can't explain where a $4,000 deposit went. The likely violation is:
options: Failing to account for money belonging to others
wrong: Steering is a fair housing violation.
why: Brokers must account for others' money.
hook: Deposit it right, record it all.

q: A busy client asks to sign a blank offer form so you can fill it in later. What should the agent do?
options: Decline; review and complete the terms with the client before they sign
Accept but email them a copy later
Have a coworker sign for them
wrong: A later copy doesn't fix it.
why: Clients sign completed documents they've reviewed.

q: After a client signs a purchase agreement, a licensee generally must:
options: Provide copies of signed documents to the parties
Send a copy to the Commission
why: Parties get copies of what they sign.

q: You notice a coworker depositing client checks into their personal account. What should the agent do?
options: Report it to your broker right away
Ignore it; it's not your client
Ask the coworker for a share
Wait until year-end to mention it
wrong: Client funds are at risk now.
That makes you part of it.
why: The broker must act on possible commingling.

q: A licensee commits three separate violations. What is the maximum total administrative fine?
why: Three violations at up to $10,000 each is $30,000.
